newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. refining market awash in Canadian heavy oil.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refining market awash in Canadian heavy oil.

text.p: The U.S. Midwest oil market is awash in Canadian heavy crude thanks to the close of the asphalt production season and new growth in heavy oil drilling, which has resulted in deep price discounting for the supply.
Traders on both sides of the border have pegged such Canadian heavies as Lloydminster and Bow River as trading at a US$9 to US$10 per barrel discount to West Texas Intermediate.

"The market is really long and, traditionally, October is when the heavy market goes into the toilet," said one Canadian marketer, who added that differentials in October have widened for at least the past five years.
This year, however, Canadian heavy oil production has increased dramatically as producers have kicked in millions of dollars to develop new heavy oil projects.
Canadian industry figures place January-to-June heavy oil production at 475,000 barrels per day, up 6.6 percent from the year before. Bitumen output was at 147,000 barrels per day, up 4.8 percent.
Also, a fire two weeks ago at British Petroleum's 155,000-barrel-per-day Toledo, Ohio refinery cut production and took some demand out of the market, traders said.
"Although it was fairly small in terms of the amount of crude impacted, it was a psychological point and people used it a lot to try to pressure the prices lower," said one.

Despite the rise in western Canadian heavy oil production, much more capacity is expected to come on stream in 1997, when the new Express pipeline to Wyoming from Alberta and expansions of the IPL Energy Inc system become operational.
Marketers on Friday said Imperial Oil Ltd's huge Cold Lake, Alberta bitumen project, which saw production cut because of frigid weather last winter, has already pumped out increased volume.

With C$450 million budgeted, Imperial aims to increase production by 30,000 barrels per day next year and another 25,000 in about three years. The project's average output was 95,000 barrels per day in 1995.
Canadian crude marketers, meanwhile, are struggling to place their high-priced light crudes amid tight pipeline space.
November apportionment on IPL's 480,000 BPD Line 2, which carries mostly light and and medium blends to the U.S. Midwest, was set at 33 percent this week, up from 23 percent for October.
Apportionment is the amount of oil expected to move on the line subtracted from shipper nominations.
Also, BC Gas Inc's Trans Mountain pipeline, which carries Canadian crudes to the West Coast, is running full out, as companies try to move their light supply players said.
IPL's 650,000 BPD Line 3, which moves mostly heavy sour crudes to the Midwest, had its November apportionment fixed at four percent, nearly unchanged from the month before.
Despite the deep discounts, heavy oil producers are still enjoying good prices for their production when compared to last year, said marketers.

In addition, output is unlikely to be cut when the differential widens because most producers would rather collect the cash flow than go through the costly process of shutting in high-tech production facilities.

"Because WTI is so high right now, a US$9 differential will put you where a US$5 differential did last year, so the producers are still enjoying life," said a Canadian trader. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
